articles.title: Brent breaks below $90 on Iran-Oman corridor talks — but Tehran says Hormuz is still shut
articles.summary: Iran and Oman discussed a temporary joint navigational corridor through Hormuz and a joint mine-clearing project, sending Brent below $90 for the first time in a week. Tehran says the deal does not mean the strait is open, and Oman's mine-clearing plan contradicts Trump's claim that all mines are already gone.
simple: Iran and Oman are talking about opening a shared shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices fell sharply — Brent went below $90 a barrel for the first time in a week.
That is good news for India, which imports more than 85% of its oil.
But Iran says the strait is still closed, and a mine-clearing project is still being planned.
Trump said on Tuesday that the US Navy had already removed every mine. Those two claims cannot both be right.

terms.meaning: The chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf that carried a fifth of global oil and LNG shipments before the war
An agreed lane through contested water that ships can use under a set of rules both sides accept
The extra amount in the oil price that reflects risk of supply disruption rather than actual supply and demand
Shorthand for the insurance and financing cost of moving cargo through a war zone — often a bigger barrier than the physical route

articles.body:
Crude fell for a second session on Wednesday after Iran and Oman said they had discussed establishing a temporary joint maritime corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, along with a joint project to clear the waterway of mines. At 10:05 IST, November Brent futures were at $85.25, down 2.31%, and October WTI at $80.30, down 2.50%. On MCX, September crude traded at ₹7,664 against a previous close of ₹7,837. ICE Brent had settled 3.89% lower on Tuesday, breaking below $90 for the first time in a week.

**What was actually agreed.** Oman's foreign minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi described talks with Iran's Abbas Araghchi in Tehran as constructive and said he hoped a corridor and "practical arrangements to restore safe navigation" would be announced soon, with "future management of the Strait and a permanent solution" to follow. The proposed framework includes joint mine clearance. Both sides are operating under a provision of the US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed on 17 June, which called for Iran and Oman to define future administration and maritime services in Hormuz. That MOU collapsed almost immediately once fighting over shipping lanes resumed.

**Three claims that do not reconcile, and this matters.** Trump said on Tuesday, on Truth Social, that all mines had been removed or detonated from international waters in Hormuz, that Space Force is "watching every square inch", and that any vessel laying new mines will be "immediately and systematically destroyed". Oman's proposal for a joint mine-clearing mission implies mines are still there. And Tehran's own line, per Al Jazeera's live coverage, is that the Oman route agreement "does not indicate that the strait is open". Do not average these. The most defensible reading is that the main southern shipping lane the US Navy protects has been cleared, while Iranian territorial waters to the north — the route Iran insists transiting ships must use or risk attack — have not been, and Iran retains the ability to reseed them.

**Why the market is discounting the good news.** ING's Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey put it plainly: any Iran-Oman agreement does not mean normalisation of flows. "We would likely need to see the US lift its blockade on Iranian ports and ease sanctions on Iran before we see any move towards normalisation." Nothing in Monday's sanctions package points that way — it points the opposite way. Meanwhile an oil tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile and disabled about nine nautical miles northeast of Oman's Ash Shishah on Monday, two cargo ships were attacked in Hormuz last week with two sailors killed, and only two commercial vessels were reported to have completed the transit on Monday. US Central Command says more than 660 million barrels have exited under its protection since May, all via the southern route.

Adding to the softness: the American Petroleum Institute reported US crude inventories rose about 4.2 million barrels in the week to 21 August, against a Reuters poll estimate of a 600,000-barrel build. EIA data follows.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** This is the most important single variable on India's macro board and it just moved in India's favour. The Indian basket averaged $89.7 a barrel in August, above both June and July; every sustained $10 down is worth roughly 0.3-0.4 percentage points on the current account deficit and takes real pressure off CPI. Tuesday's equity rally, the rupee's 32-34 paise gain to 95.41 and the softening in bond yields all trace to the same source. OMCs — IOC, BPCL, HPCL — are the direct marketing-margin beneficiaries; paints, tyres, aviation and logistics get input relief. Upstream producers ONGC and Oil India move the other way.

**Keep the base rate in mind.** Crude is still up around 45% this year, the war is in its sixth month, and Fujitomi's Mitsuru Muraishi expects prices to stay range-bound as bargain buying limits the fall. A corridor announcement would be a genuine de-escalation signal; a corridor that Iran simultaneously describes as not opening the strait is a negotiating position.

**What to watch.** Whether a corridor is formally announced and on which route, EIA inventory data, tanker-tracking transit counts, and whether Washington pairs sanctions escalation with any blockade relief.

articles.title: 'Operation Economic Outcast' names four Indian firms — and 24 Chinese ones
articles.as_of: US State Department / Treasury designations announced Monday 2026-08-24; Chinese designations reported 2026-08-26
articles.summary: Washington sanctioned four India-based companies and three Indian nationals for importing Iranian petroleum products, plus 24 entities in mainland China and Hong Kong. Beijing called the measures illegal and vowed 'all necessary measures'. No Chinese bank was designated — Bessent: 'Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?'
simple: The US has sanctioned four Indian companies for importing Iranian oil products worth about $120 million.
It also sanctioned 24 companies in China and Hong Kong.
China called the sanctions illegal and said it will protect its interests.
The US deliberately did not sanction any Chinese bank — that would risk breaking the global financial system.
India's actual exports to Iran are small (~$1.25bn, mostly basmati rice) so direct trade damage is limited.

terms.meaning: Penalties on third-country firms for dealing with a sanctioned country, rather than on the sanctioned country itself
Being added to the US Treasury's Specially Designated Nationals list — assets frozen, and US persons barred from dealing with you
The Iranian port where India operates the Shahid Beheshti terminal, its route to Afghanistan and Central Asia bypassing Pakistan
When banks cut off entire categories of client to avoid sanctions exposure — usually a bigger effect than the designations themselves

articles.body:
The US widened its Iran sanctions campaign to India on Monday. The State Department designated Portease Partners LLP, an India-based customs broker, for facilitating multiple shipments of Iranian petrochemical products into India, along with its partners Indrismiya Ashrafmiya Shekh and Harish Ramchandra Rangi. Three other India-based companies were also targeted: Sadashiva Overseas Ltd, which Washington says imported about $69 million of Iranian-origin petroleum products between February 2024 and June 2025; PP Softtech Pvt Ltd, linked to roughly $25 million between January 2024 and June 2025, whose director Prashant Garg was separately designated; and Prakrutees Infra Impex India Pvt Ltd, about $25 million between May 2023 and February 2026.

Roughly 60 entities, individuals and vessels were designated in the round, covering Iran's oil and petrochemical revenues, shipping, banking, technology, gold, aviation and digital assets. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent framed it: "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone." By Wednesday, SCMP reported a further 24 entities based in mainland China or Hong Kong had been added under the same campaign.

**India's official posture is wait-and-see.** "It is not yet clear what kind of sanctions these are. The notification is awaited," a source tracking the matter told businessline. "The government would keep an eye on how the development plays out before deciding on its response." That restraint is telling. New Delhi is simultaneously handing over operations of the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar — a strategic asset the US has historically carved out of Iran sanctions — and cannot afford to make this a public confrontation.

**The direct trade exposure is genuinely small.** India stopped buying Iranian crude in 2019 and its FY26 exports to Iran were $1.25 billion, of which basmati rice alone was $810.08 million, against $11.5 billion of total Indian rice exports. Imports from Iran were about $375 million. All India Rice Exporters Association general secretary Ajay Bhalothia says Iranian demand has held up through the war on food-security grounds, with Tehran buying over one million tonnes of rice in FY26 against 855,132 tonnes a year earlier, and that exporters have built payment channels through Dubai and the wider UAE, Germany, China and most recently Turkey which have not been disrupted. Pharmaceuticals, tea, bananas, cereals and bovine meat also benefit from humanitarian exceptions.

**The real risk is not trade, it is banking.** The $120 million cited across the three importers is trivial against India's trade flows. What matters is that Washington is now designating intermediaries — customs brokers, importers, shipping and financial firms — rather than only Iranian entities. Indian banks and logistics providers will respond by de-risking: refusing categories of business that carry any Iran nexus, whether or not it is sanctioned. That is a compliance-cost story that lands on legitimate exporters, and it is why the government is being careful.

**China is the test case Washington is avoiding.** Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China "firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions" and will "take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests". China buys an estimated 80% of Iran's oil exports. Yet no Chinese financial institution appeared on the list despite their role in financing that trade. Asked why, Bessent replied: "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?" That single sentence is the honest boundary of the campaign. A Trump-Xi summit is scheduled next month, and Beijing controls the majority of the world's rare-earth processing — leverage it has already used in trade talks. Iran's economy minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared", with a two-year plan.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** Watch compliance costs and banking friction at trading houses, customs brokers, shipping and port-logistics firms with any West Asia exposure. The bigger read-through is macro: sanctions that do not actually stop Chinese purchases keep Iranian barrels flowing, which is part of why crude fell rather than rose on the announcement. Markets judged the package less severe than feared.

**What to watch.** Whether any Chinese bank is designated, the formal Indian notification, and Chabahar's carve-out status.

articles.title: Bitcoin tops $80,000 for the first time since May as the debasement trade returns
articles.summary: Bitcoin rose as much as 2.9% to $81,257, its first move above $80,000 since mid-May, after Bessent's expanded bond buybacks weakened the dollar and revived the debasement trade. Spot ETFs drew a net $1.92bn last week, the most since early October.
simple: Bitcoin went above $80,000 for the first time since mid-May.
The cause was not crypto news — it was the US Treasury buying back its own long-term bonds, which weakened the dollar.
That revived the 'debasement trade': buying gold and bitcoin when you distrust government finances.
US bitcoin ETFs took in $1.92 billion last week, the most in ten months.
Bitcoin is still far below its October record of about $126,000.

terms.meaning: Buying hard assets — gold, bitcoin — on the view that governments will inflate away their debts rather than repay them in real terms
The average price over the last 50 weeks; technical traders treat a close above it as confirmation of a trend change
Forced closing of leveraged bets against the price, which requires buying — and so accelerates the rally
Coins that have not moved in over a year; the higher the share, the less is actually available to trade

articles.body:
Bitcoin climbed above $80,000 for the first time since mid-May, rising as much as 2.9% to $81,257 on Tuesday before easing to around $79,300 by 06:30 in New York. The move capped a 23% gain over the seven days to Sunday — the largest weekly jump in about three years — and forced the liquidation of billions of dollars of leveraged short positions.

**The catalyst is a bond story, not a crypto story.** Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's announcement that the US would step up repurchases of long-dated government debt to bring down long-term yields triggered a fresh round of dollar selling. Sceptics read the plan as evidence the administration is not prepared to do the harder work of shrinking the deficit — which is precisely the thesis bitcoin was built on. "The macro backdrop turned more supportive after the Treasury's expanded long-dated buyback plan helped weaken the dollar and revive the 'debasement trade' across Bitcoin and gold," said Lacie Zhang, research analyst at Bitget Wallet. Gold rallied on the same logic and for the same reason, which is the cleanest confirmation that this is a monetary-credibility trade rather than a sector rotation.

**Institutional flow has genuinely returned.** The 13 US-listed spot bitcoin ETFs drew a net $1.92 billion last week, their strongest weekly inflow in ten months and the most since early October last year, with a further $337 million on Monday. That demand is colliding with tight float: roughly 60% of circulating bitcoin has not moved in more than a year. Fixed supply meeting returning demand is the mechanical part of the move; the short squeeze is the accelerant.

**The level traders are watching.** Bitcoin has been approaching its 50-week moving average of roughly $81,000, a threshold it has traded below since November. "A close above this WMA level would be further constructive on a continuing bull rally," said Rajiv Sawhney, head of international portfolio management at Wave Digital Assets. Tuesday's high touched it and the close did not hold it. Until it does, this remains a rally inside a downtrend.

**Keep the drawdown in view.** The token peaked near $126,000 in October. At $80,000 it is still down roughly a third from that high, after months of sideways trading. Recovering to a level last seen in May is not the same as a new cycle, and the honest framing is that bitcoin is currently trading as a high-beta expression of US fiscal credibility — which means it can reverse just as fast if the Treasury's buyback programme is judged to have failed. Stanley Druckenmiller and others are already making exactly that argument in public.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The tax regime has not changed: 30% on gains, 1% TDS on transfers, no loss set-off. That makes momentum trading structurally expensive here regardless of the price, and it is the single most important fact for an Indian participant. The more useful transferable signal is directional — if you believe the debasement thesis, the same view is expressible through gold, which is available in Indian markets in ETF, sovereign-bond and futures form with far better tax treatment, and which rallied on identical news. Buying the thesis does not require buying the token.

**What to watch.** Whether bitcoin closes a week above $81,000, whether ETF inflows persist past one strong week, the dollar index, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech on Friday — the same event that will set gold's direction.

Canada is also giving C$7.5 billion in support to affected businesses and workers.

articles.body:
Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on C$27.6 billion ($19.94 billion) of United States goods on Tuesday, matching Washington's latest duties dollar-for-dollar, and unveiled a C$7.5 billion package to support businesses and workers caught in the escalation. The counter-tariffs take effect on 8 September across roughly 700 products at three rates: 50% on steel, aluminium, furniture and clothing; 25% on cheese, appliances and some seafood; 15% on electronics and tools.

"Our dollar-for-dollar, rate for rate counter-tariffs as well as a multi-billion dollar support package will protect workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said, characterising the response as "proportionate" and "strategic". A government official said the list was designed so that the impact on Canadian consumers and businesses is minimal while still hitting US exporters.

**How this happened.** Trade talks between the two countries collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of last-minute unreasonable demands. Trump's new 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian imports took effect on Saturday. Canada's response followed on Tuesday. The Conservative opposition in Ottawa has asked for the full text of the draft deal to be released, and questions remain about exactly why the negotiation failed. Polls suggest most Canadians support holding firm.

**Why this is worse than the numbers suggest.** The US and Canada are among the most deeply integrated economies in the world, with supply chains built over decades across manufacturing, energy, agriculture and autos. In an integrated chain a component may cross the border several times before final assembly, and a tariff applies at each crossing — so a 50% headline rate on steel compounds far beyond 50% by the time it reaches a finished good. Both sides' businesses and consumers absorb it. The product selection also tells you something: Canada picked categories where domestic or third-country substitutes exist, which limits self-harm but also limits the pressure it applies.

**The rhetoric is now the risk.** Relations have deteriorated to the point where Trump has floated renaming Lake Ontario "Lake America", and Ontario Premier Doug Ford has said the US is treating Canada "like Communist China". Prime Minister Mark Carney — a former central bank governor who ran both the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England — is not a leader who can domestically afford to fold. When both sides have made retreat politically expensive, the escalation ladder has no natural exit.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** No direct exposure, but three read-throughs. First, this is a live demonstration of how the current US administration handles a trade negotiation that stalls — relevant as India works through its own US trade discussions alongside the EU pact. Second, tariff walls between the two largest North American economies redirect trade flows, and Indian exporters in steel, aluminium, apparel and furniture may find both incremental opportunity in the US market and incremental competition from Canadian goods seeking new homes. Third, and most immediately, escalating trade fragmentation is one of the two forces the RBI's own bulletin named as shaping the global outlook — the other being West Asia. It feeds the term-premium and growth-risk story that runs through global bond markets.

**What to watch.** Whether the 8 September date holds or becomes a negotiating deadline, whether the US responds with a further round, USMCA review politics, and the Canadian dollar.

articles.title: RBI flags second-round inflation risk as Q1 growth is seen slowing to 7.1%
articles.as_of: RBI August Bulletin released 2026-08-25; Reuters poll of 58 economists, 17-24 August; GDP data due 2026-08-31
sources_checked: RBI August Bulletin / State of the Economy report
articles.summary: Governor Malhotra warned in the August Bulletin that second-round effects of higher food, fuel and input prices could turn into broad-based inflation. Food prices rose broadly through 21 August despite the monsoon recovery. A Reuters poll sees Q1 GDP at 7.1%, down from 7.8%.

India would still be the world's fastest-growing major economy.

Inflation excluding food and fuel — the RBI watches it to judge whether a shock is spreading
Fast-arriving data (e-way bills, PMI, fuel sales) used to read the economy before official statistics land

articles.body:
Two documents landed within a day of each other and they say the same thing from opposite ends: the economy is holding up, and the inflation risk is not behind us.

**The Bulletin.** "Although generalised inflation pressures continue to remain modest so far, the risks of second-round impact of higher food, fuel and other input prices translating to broad-based inflation persist," Governor Sanjay Malhotra wrote in the August Bulletin. Headline CPI was 4.5% in July against 4.4% in June — above the 4% medium-term target, driven by supply-side pressure, with stable core inflation indicating limited pass-through so far. That last clause is doing a lot of work. Core stability is what separates a supply shock from an inflation cycle, and it is exactly what the MPC minutes released last week said members were watching, having warned that a sustained broad-based rise would create pressure for tightening.

**The State of the Economy report.** Prepared by RBI economists under Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta, it found a broad-based sequential increase in food prices in high-frequency data through 21 August — even as the southwest monsoon recovery brought kharif sowing close to normal acreage and partly mitigated agricultural risk. Note the tension: the monsoon fixed the supply story and food prices rose anyway. July's high-frequency indicators showed sustained manufacturing and services activity and double-digit growth in both merchandise exports and imports, with rural demand supporting consumption. The merchandise trade deficit widened year-on-year and sequentially, driven by electronic goods; the oil deficit was unchanged even though the Indian basket averaged $89.7 a barrel in August, above both June and July. The report names the two external forces shaping the outlook — West Asian geopolitical friction and fresh US tariffs — while arguing India's macro fundamentals provide a cushion.

**The growth print.** A Reuters poll of 58 economists conducted 17-24 August puts April-June GDP growth at 7.1%, slowing from a better-than-expected 7.8%, with forecasts ranging from 6.2% to 8.0%. Data lands on 31 August. Consumer spending and government expenditure carry the quarter; private investment is the weak leg. "We started seeing some sort of a nascent recovery in private investment since the second half of last year but it is yet to become stronger, more durable and more broad-based," said HDFC Bank principal economist Sakshi Gupta. "The conflict perhaps made private players a little bit more cautious with their outlook, in terms of their capacity expansion plans in certain sectors." Last year's GST rate cut and income tax reductions are still supporting household disposable income.

**Put the three together.** Growth is decelerating but remains the fastest among major economies. Inflation is drifting up from subdued levels on supply shocks that have not yet spread. Private capex is hesitant because of war-driven uncertainty. That combination is why the RBI is signalling rather than acting — it has room to wait, and waiting costs it little while core holds.

**The variable that decides it.** India imports more than 85% of its oil. Crude above $90 raises household fuel and transport costs and business input costs simultaneously. Which is why this week's break below $90 on Iran-Oman corridor talks matters more to the RBI's October decision than any domestic datapoint. A sustained retreat towards $80 removes the second-round risk the Governor named; a return above $95 makes it live.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The rate path is now genuinely two-sided, and it is being decided in the Strait of Hormuz. Duration risk in long gilt funds is real but has just improved. On equities, the growth composition — consumption and government spending carrying it, private capex lagging — argues for consumption-facing and government-order-book names over broad industrial capex plays until private investment confirms.

**What to watch.** The 31 August GDP print, August CPI in mid-September, and Brent.

articles.title: Druckenmiller turns on his own protégé: 'Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination'
articles.as_of: Druckenmiller WSJ op-ed and market reaction, 2026-08-25
articles.summary: Stanley Druckenmiller — Bessent's own investing mentor — used a WSJ op-ed to urge him to abandon the 19 August buyback plan and let the bond market price freely. Meanwhile options traders bought over 175,000 TLT calls on Tuesday against fewer than 40,000 puts.

His argument: the real problem is the deficit, and hiding it just delays the reckoning.

The budget gap before interest payments — the part a government can actually control through tax and spending

Buying one call and selling a higher-strike call — a cheaper, capped bet that the price rises

articles.body:
Scott Bessent's bond-market interventions have produced a modest decline in yields and a rapidly growing chorus of critics. The most pointed of them is Stanley Druckenmiller — head of Duquesne Family Office and, more to the point, Bessent's own investing mentor. The two, with George Soros, famously orchestrated the bet against the pound in the early 1990s.

In a Wall Street Journal op-ed titled "Let the Bond Market Speak", Druckenmiller urged Bessent to abandon the buyback scheme announced on 19 August and let the market set the price of government debt free of the government's hand. "If the 30-year must trade at 5.5% to clear, that isn't a crisis. It is an invoice," he wrote. "Then do the only thing that durably lowers long-term yields: address the primary deficit."

The mechanism of his objection is the part worth understanding. "Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination. Once markets believe Treasury is defending a price, every rise in yields becomes a test of official resolve, and the operations must grow to survive the tests." And the conclusion: "Governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose. The only variable is how much they spend before conceding."

**The scale problem is real.** Wall Street has been broadly sceptical that Treasury has the firepower to manage a market that absorbed some $4.8 trillion of issuance in 2025 alone, a level that could be exceeded this year. Total debt has just passed $40 trillion, and the budget deficit is heading above $2 trillion for 2026. Against that, doubling a $2 billion-per-operation buyback programme is a small instrument. Bessent has also intervened in currency markets — supporting the yen in late July so the Bank of Japan would not have to sell Treasuries, which would have pushed US yields higher. Two interventions in a month is a pattern, and patterns invite testing.

**What has actually happened so far.** The efforts have pushed longer-dated yields off peaks that were the highest since before the 2008 financial crisis. The 30-year reached 19-year highs last week. The 10-year, notably, remains below both its January 2025 high and the 5% level it pierced in 2023 — so the stress is concentrated at the very long end, which is where supply and term premium bite hardest.

**The market is not siding with Druckenmiller yet.** Options traders in TLT, the long-duration Treasury ETF, have been buying bullish calls almost all summer, and continued on Tuesday: more than 175,000 calls traded against fewer than 40,000 puts. One trader bought 10,000 November-20 85-strike calls for $1 million and sold 15,000 of the 90-strike calls expiring the same day for $375,000 — a call spread with a maximum payout 8% higher, at levels unseen since March. That is a substantial wager that long yields fall further. Positioning and the loudest analytical voice are pointing in opposite directions.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The US long end is the global term-premium anchor, and it currently sets the cost of capital for everything from Indian corporate borrowing abroad to FPI allocation decisions to the valuation of debt-funded AI infrastructure. It is also why gold and bitcoin rallied this week and why Indian bonds got some relief. The Druckenmiller argument, if it wins, means the relief is temporary and the 30-year has further to rise. That is a genuine two-sided risk sitting under every asset class right now — including Indian equities, where FPI flows respond to exactly this variable.

**What to watch.** Whether the 30-year holds below recent peaks through the buyback operations, Treasury's next quarterly refunding for the issuance mix, and whether any Treasury official responds to the op-ed. The department did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

articles.body:
Gold and silver futures opened higher on Wednesday, extending a rally that has become one of the year's cleanest macro trades. On MCX the benchmark October gold contract opened at ₹1,63,202 per 10 grams, up ₹320 from the previous close of ₹1,62,882, trading at ₹1,63,136 with a session range of ₹1,62,021 to ₹1,63,202. September silver opened at ₹2,45,583 per kg, up ₹1,456, and traded at ₹2,45,700. On Comex, gold opened at $4,715.70 against $4,694.50 and traded at $4,705.40; silver traded at $69.18. Bloomberg had spot bullion around $4,660 at 07:35 Singapore time, close to a three-month high, up more than 7% in a week.

**Two forces are pushing the same way.** First, the US Treasury's expanded buybacks of long-dated debt sent yields down five to seven basis points across the curve on Tuesday and weakened the dollar — cutting gold's opportunity cost and reviving the debasement trade that powered last year's record rally, when investors bought bullion to avoid sovereign debt and currencies. Second, oil fell on Iran-Oman de-escalation talks, which eases inflation pressure and so reduces the odds the Fed has to hike — and higher borrowing costs are the main headwind for non-yielding bullion. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said she supported holding rates steady for now provided inflation progress continues.

**The demand data is the durable part.** World Gold Council figures show about 23 tonnes added to global ETF holdings recently, with flows accelerating to 45 tonnes month-to-date in August. Central banks bought 288.9 tonnes in the second quarter, a 62% increase year-on-year, and South Korea returned to the gold market after 13 years. The WGC's Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey found 89% of respondents expect global reserves to rise over the next year and a record 45% expect to increase their own holdings. Reserve diversification, crisis performance and protection against geopolitical risk continue to dominate official-sector thinking. This is buying that does not care about the price.

**Keep the year in view.** Gold surged past $5,500 in January, then tumbled to $4,600 by August as the Iran war sent oil soaring and fuelled expectations the Fed could raise rates. The current 15% one-month rebound is the strongest in over four months but leaves the metal about 16% below its peak. Jefferies' Christopher Wood and John Paulson remain bullish on both bullion and gold miners.

**The swing factor is on Friday.** Kevin Warsh's first major speech as Fed chairman, at Jackson Hole, is the near-term determinant — an opportunity to answer criticism that he has not been forthright about his economic views. US PCE data lands Wednesday. A hawkish Warsh, or a hot PCE print, caps this rally; a dovish one extends it.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** Note the rupee leg. The currency gained 32-34 paise to 95.41 on Tuesday with RBI support, and a stronger rupee mechanically dampens the MCX price relative to Comex — which is why domestic gains have lagged the dollar move. For allocation, sovereign gold bonds and gold ETFs give the exposure without making-charge and purity friction, and with better tax treatment than physical. Listed gold financiers — Muthoot, Manappuram, IIFL Finance — are the leveraged operating play: higher gold prices lift collateral values and loan demand, but they carry RBI regulatory risk on LTV and disbursal norms that is entirely uncorrelated with the metal. Separately, Kotak's Nilesh Shah floated a gold-backed stablecoin this week as a way to cut India's import bill — an idea worth tracking rather than trading.

**What to watch.** Warsh at Jackson Hole on Friday, US PCE, the $4,600 level on spot, and festive physical demand as Onam passes and Ganesh Chaturthi through Diwali approaches.

articles.body:
The Department of Homeland Security proposed on Monday to make permanent an additional fee of $103,265 on all H-1B cap-subject applications, including those eligible for the advanced-degree exemption. The current fee runs between $2,000 and $5,000. Public comments are invited over 30 days.

**The legal position is unsettled.** Trump raised the cost of H-1B visas to $100,000 last year, prompting several lawsuits. A federal judge ruled in June that the fee was illegal and blocked its collection; a Boston-based appeals court is reviewing that decision, and another court is considering whether a judge properly rejected a challenge by the US Chamber of Commerce, the largest US business lobby. Democratic-led states and a coalition of unions and employers have also sued. The initial increase is set to expire in September — which is precisely why DHS is now attempting a permanent version through formal rulemaking rather than executive action. Pending cases could be amended to challenge the new rule once finalised.

**Who this actually hits.** Indians accounted for an estimated 71% of approved H-1B applications in recent years. Top sponsors include Deloitte, PwC and Ernst & Young alongside Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, HCL Tech and LTIMindtree — and also Tesla, Amazon and OpenAI, all of which have faced questions over visa use amid US layoffs and a tighter job market for American workers.

**Nasscom's response is the interesting one, because it is a concession.** The industry body said the proposed increase "must be viewed in the context of the programme's original purpose of enabling access to temporary skills where there is a shortage in the US" — and then noted that over the past five years the number of H-1B employees at Indian technology companies "has reduced significantly, as companies have steadily expanded local hiring". It pointed to more than $1.1 billion invested in strengthening the US STEM pipeline, partnerships with over 130 universities and colleges, 2.9 million students impacted and 255,000 employees upskilled. This is not a defence of the visa; it is an argument that Indian IT no longer needs it much. That is both a real structural shift — offshore delivery and US local hiring have replaced visa-dependent onsite staffing — and a negotiating posture.

**The counter-argument.** The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies warns the fee would push US jobs overseas. "A USD 103,265 H-1B fee could choke cash-strapped startups, while companies hiring thousands of H-1B workers could face hundreds of millions of dollars — and potentially close to a billion dollars — in additional costs," said policy chief Khanderao Kand. Combined with a potential $100,000 OPT fee, totalling $203,265, he argues the student-to-work pathway becomes effectively unaffordable. FIIDS notes new international student enrolment fell 17% in autumn 2025, and cites a NAFSA projection of up to 111,000 fewer international students — a 9.5% decline and an economic loss of up to $3.4 billion. It also points out USCIS already receives around 96% of its funding from applicant fees, undercutting the revenue rationale.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** For the listed Indian IT majors this is a manageable headwind rather than a shock, precisely for the reason Nasscom gave — the visa-linked cost base has already shrunk, and the sector's live problem is AI-driven price deflation, with Hexaware's CEO warning this week that AI will deflate the value of IT work by up to 25% and firms turning to bundled deals in response. The sharper impact is on the talent pipeline: fewer Indian students entering the US means more staying, which strengthens the case for India's GCC boom, where 52% of GCCs plan workforce expansion in FY27. For individuals weighing a US master's as a career route, the arithmetic has genuinely changed.

**What to watch.** The comment period outcome, the Boston appeals court ruling, and whether the OPT fee proposal materialises.

articles.body:
Air India is seeking about $1.5 billion in fresh equity from its owners, Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters — one of the largest publicly reported shareholder funding requests since Tata took control of the former state-owned carrier in 2022.

The trigger is the scale of the loss. Air India and its budget unit Air India Express posted combined losses of $2.33 billion in the financial year ended March, more than double the prior year's, a figure that has also weighed on Singapore Airlines' own profits. "Air India wants the funds immediately, though the infusion is likely to happen in tranches. Singapore Airlines would need to contribute its share of the proposed infusion for the investment to go through," one source said. Discussions are ongoing and no decision has been taken. Air India and Tata Sons did not respond to Reuters. Singapore Airlines, which owns around 25%, said it was working closely with Tata Sons to support the transformation programme but declined to comment on the airline's finances.

**Why the losses doubled.** Four distinct pressures landed at once, and only one of them is management's doing. Pakistan's airspace ban on Indian carriers forces longer routings to Europe and North America, adding fuel burn and crew hours on exactly the long-haul routes that are supposed to be the profit engine. The US-Israeli war with Iran has disrupted the international network through the same airspace corridor and kept fuel expensive for most of the year. Last year's crash, which killed 260 people, carries costs that run well past insurance. And underneath all of it sits the multi-billion-dollar revamp itself — refurbishing a legacy fleet, replacing systems, retraining people — which consumes cash years before it produces returns.

**The turnaround was always going to be long.** Chandrasekaran has said publicly that it could take up to a decade, citing persistent supply-chain disruption and the need to overhaul the airline's legacy systems, culture and fleet. Air India has already sought to defer deliveries of hundreds of jets on order from Airbus and Boeing as Tata presses for cost cuts. "Air India is expected to continue requiring capital infusions in the coming years," one source said — which is the sentence that matters most for anyone modelling this.

**The governance overlay.** The request comes as Tata Sons chair N. Chandrasekaran prepares to step down in February, following months of disagreement with the group's controlling charitable trust, partly over Air India's losses. A capital call of this size, arriving while the chairman who authored the acquisition strategy is on his way out, means the decision will be taken in an unusually contested boardroom. Singapore Airlines' participation is the practical constraint: SIA is a listed company answerable to its own shareholders for an investment that is currently a drag on reported profit.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** There is no direct listed exposure to Air India, but there are three real read-throughs. Singapore Airlines shareholders are funding this. Indian aviation's competitive structure is affected — a recapitalised Air India competes harder with IndiGo, while a capital-constrained one cedes share, and IndiGo is the listed way to express either view. And airport operators, ground handlers and MRO providers are exposed to Air India's capacity plans, which the deferral requests suggest are being trimmed.

**For anyone working in or entering Indian aviation.** A carrier consuming capital at this rate manages headcount and vendor contracts tightly, but it is also mid-way through the largest fleet and systems overhaul in the country's aviation history — which is where the hiring actually is. Read the deferrals as a signal on capacity growth, not on the transformation programme itself.

**What to watch.** Whether Singapore Airlines commits, the tranche structure and any milestones attached, further delivery deferrals, and who succeeds Chandrasekaran.

articles.body:
The government's sugar intervention worked faster than anyone expected, and it has produced an unusual second-order problem.

**What happened.** Ex-mill sugar prices have fallen 18% to ₹55 per kg from a record ₹67 last week, Food Secretary Sanjeev Chopra told PTI. He attributed the spike to mills "jacking up" rates rather than to fundamentals: production for the 2025-26 marketing year fell to 306 lakh tonnes against an earlier estimate of 343 lakh, but annual domestic demand is only around 280-285 lakh tonnes, and stocks are ample. "Ex-mill price of sugar, which were jacked up by mills, have started cooling down. They have declined to ₹55 per kg and will further drop in the coming days."

The trigger was a three-part package last week: duty-free import of 1 million tonnes of raw sugar under the Tariff Rate Quota until end-October, stock limits on bulk consumers, and instructions to states to intensify inspections against hoarding. Flying squads were deployed nationwide. National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories MD Prakash Naiknavare says no state now has ex-mill prices above ₹55.

**The consumer has not felt it yet.** Naiknavare notes the typical gap of ₹2-3/kg between ex-mill and wholesale and ₹7-8/kg between ex-mill and retail. Average all-India wholesale was still ₹58.29/kg and retail ₹63.05/kg on 24 August, per Consumer Affairs Ministry data. Retail prices in fact rose by nearly ₹1 to about ₹64 in separate reporting this week. The ex-mill correction takes weeks to travel down the chain, and it may not travel fully.

**The government tightened the screws again on Tuesday.** DGFT Lav Agarwal amended the 20 August public notice, which had merely required imported raw sugar to be refined "within a reasonable period" and sold by 31 October. The revised text is definite: importers must convert the raw sugar to white or refined sugar and sell it domestically "within a period, not exceeding two months, from the date of filing of bill of entry". The Food Ministry pushed for this because the whole point of allowing imports was to augment availability, and an open-ended timeline invites warehousing rather than selling.

**And here is the twist.** Having crushed the price, the government may find nobody wants the quota. Mills and refiners are likely to import only about half the permitted million tonnes, industry officials told Reuters, because falling domestic prices have destroyed the import margin. "Imports looked attractive last week, when prices were firm and rising. But the sharp price drop since the announcement has taken the shine off imports for millers," said Rahil Shaikh, MD of Mumbai-based MEIR Commodities. "The import margin is thin, and there is no guarantee it will hold when shipments arrive in nearly two months." Shaikh and four other dealers put likely imports below 500,000 tonnes, with most taken by port-based refineries — which could quickly release around 300,000 tonnes of existing stock domestically. Mills have no interest, because domestic supplies rise from mid-October when the new crushing season starts, which India has advanced to 15 October.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The announcement itself did the work; the imports may barely be needed. That is a textbook demonstration of expectations management in a commodity market, and it is bad for sugar equities — the trade was long a price spike that the government has now demonstrated it will not tolerate. Dolat Capital still sees up to 25% upside in two sugar names, but the policy asymmetry is unattractive: mills capture upside only until the government intervenes, and the government has just shown how quickly it does. FMCG and confectionery buyers are the relative winners into the festive quarter. On the macro side, this is a visible win against exactly the food-price pressure the RBI Bulletin flagged on the same day.

**What to watch.** Actual TRQ utilisation against the 1mn tonne allowance, whether retail follows ex-mill down, and cane crushing volumes from 15 October.

articles.title: Adani Energy wins a ₹4,700-crore Maharashtra transmission line built for pumped storage

articles.summary: Adani Energy Solutions won 'Network Expansion Scheme in Western Region to Cater to Pumped Storage Potential near Satara (up to 4500 MW) - Part A' through competitive bidding. The ₹4,700-crore project adds 562 ckm and 9,000 MVA over 36 months. Shares opened at a gap up of ₹1,617.

articles.body:
Adani Energy Solutions has won a transmission project for evacuating renewable energy generated in Karnataka to major load centres in Maharashtra, at an estimated capital expenditure of about ₹4,700 crore. The project — formally "Network Expansion Scheme in Western Region to Cater to Pumped Storage Potential near Satara (up to 4500 MW) - Part A" — was awarded through Tariff Based Competitive Bidding, with AESL emerging as the lowest bidder. It will be housed under a special purpose vehicle, Satara Power Transmission, and delivered within 36 months, adding 562 circuit kilometres of lines and 9,000 MVA of transformation capacity. That takes AESL's cumulative network to 29,739 ckm and 1,43,425 MVA. Shares opened with an upside gap at ₹1,617 on the NSE and touched ₹1,634.90 within minutes of the opening bell.

**Read the project name — it tells you what this actually is.** This is not a generic transmission line. It is infrastructure built specifically to serve up to 4,500 MW of pumped storage potential near Satara, while carrying Karnataka renewables to the Satara, Pune and Mumbai Metropolitan Region load centres. Pumped storage is the piece India's renewable build-out has been missing. Solar generates at midday and demand peaks in the evening; without storage, either the solar is curtailed or thermal plants must cycle to fill the gap. Pumped storage — water pumped uphill during the solar surplus and released through turbines at peak — is the only grid-scale storage technology India can deploy at gigawatt scale today at acceptable cost. Maharashtra's Western Ghats topography makes Satara one of the better sites in the country.

But a pumped storage plant is worthless without wires to the load centre. Transmission has to be built ahead of the storage, and the storage ahead of the renewable capacity it firms. This award is the first link in that chain being laid.

**What it means for the business.** Transmission under TBCB is a regulated-return, availability-linked annuity business: once built, the asset earns a tariff for carrying capacity whether or not power flows, over a concession measured in decades. The risk sits almost entirely in execution — right-of-way acquisition, forest and wildlife clearances through the Ghats, and commodity costs on conductor and steel over a 36-month build. Winning as lowest bidder means the return is thin if execution slips. AESL's existing 29,739 ckm base is the argument that it will not.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** Two things. First, this is a straightforward addition to a visible, contracted, long-duration cash flow stream — the most predictable part of the Adani group's portfolio and the part least exposed to the group's financing controversies. Second, and more broadly, the transmission-plus-storage build-out is emerging as one of the clearest multi-year capex themes in India, and it runs through a small set of players: AESL and Power Grid on transmission, plus the EPC contractors and conductor, cable and transformer suppliers underneath them. Titagarh, Kalpataru, GR Infraprojects and the cable makers all sit in that chain. A project explicitly sized to a 4,500 MW pumped storage cluster is a signal about the pipeline behind it.

**Context from the same week.** PFC and REC — the two dedicated power-sector lenders that finance most of this — were downgraded by Morgan Stanley last week on loan growth concerns, a useful reminder that the capex theme and the financing of it are separate trades.

**What to watch.** Financial closure and clearance timelines for the SPV, the corresponding pumped storage awards near Satara, and whether Part B of the scheme is tendered.

articles.title: Hindustan Copper OFS oversubscribed 3.41x on day one — and the government signals more PSU sales

sources_checked: DIPAM Secretary Arunish Chawla via X
articles.summary: The government's Hindustan Copper OFS drew institutional bids of 3.41x on day one at a floor of ₹514 — over 10% below the prior close — prompting full exercise of the greenshoe. Retail bid on Wednesday with the stock up over 3%. FY27 disinvestment target: ₹80,000 crore, ~₹52,000 crore raised.

So the government exercised its option to sell an extra 3%, taking the total to 6%.
The stock fell 7% on Tuesday to ₹533.20 because of the discounted supply, then rose over 3% Wednesday.
The government has a ₹80,000 crore asset-sale target this year and has raised about ₹52,000 crore.

articles.body:
The government's offer for sale in Hindustan Copper drew bids of 3.41 times the shares on offer from institutional investors on the opening day, prompting the Centre to exercise the entire greenshoe option. "The government will now sell the additional shares available under the green-shoe option," DIPAM Secretary Arunish Chawla posted on X. Retail investors and eligible employees bid on Wednesday, with 10% of the offer reserved for retail and up to 25,000 shares earmarked for employees. The stock rose over 3% on Wednesday morning.

**The mechanics.** The government offered 3% of Hindustan Copper — 29 million shares — with an option to sell another 3%, taking the potential total to 6%. The floor price of ₹514 represented a more than 10% discount to the previous close, which is what produced both the strong book and the selling pressure: the stock closed 7% lower at ₹533.20 on the BSE on Tuesday. At the floor price, the full 6% would realise about ₹2,982 crore. The government held 63.96 crore shares, or 66.14%, at the end of the June quarter; a full 6% sale takes it to 60.14%. At Monday's close of ₹573.55 the government's stake was worth roughly ₹36,685 crore against a total market capitalisation of about ₹55,464 crore.

**Understand what a 3.41x book at a 10% discount actually tells you.** Not much about Hindustan Copper. An OFS priced meaningfully below market will almost always clear, because the discount itself is the return — institutions can bid, receive allotment and sell into the market for the spread. The information content is in how the stock trades in the weeks after the flowback, not on subscription day. The 7% fall on Tuesday and the 3% bounce on Wednesday are both mostly mechanical.

**The fiscal picture is the real story.** The Centre has a FY27 disinvestment target of ₹80,000 crore and has already mobilised around ₹52,000 crore, including the LIC OFS and this transaction. Chawla says the government will meet it: "We are working hard and we will achieve the target, and we will continue to work hard," while adding that the focus is not solely on numerical targets. Mint reported on 10 August that the Centre had already raised nearly three-fourths of the target — a goal it has repeatedly missed in recent years. Making it this early, this comfortably, is genuinely new.

**And more is coming.** Chawla indicated further market offerings will follow without naming candidates. Separately, the Centre has outlined Asset Monetisation Pipeline 2.0, covering highways, railways, power, ports, mining and other infrastructure over five years. Note what this programme is and is not: these are minority stake sales through OFS, executed without transferring management control. It is a fiscal exercise, not privatisation, and it does not change how these companies are run.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** Two practical implications. First, expect a steady supply of discounted PSU paper over the coming months — which caps upside in the PSU names most likely to be tapped, since a known future seller sitting on 60-70% of the register is an overhang regardless of fundamentals. Screen PSU holdings for high residual government stakes and a plausible fiscal need. Second, the OFS discount is a recurring, semi-predictable opportunity for investors able to participate, but the flowback risk is real and the trade is a spread capture, not a view on the company.

**Related, and worth reading together.** A separate report this week said the government is weighing further stake sales as the disinvestment drive stays active; Mint also reported the OFS was expanded amid the strong demand.

**What to watch.** Retail subscription numbers, where the stock settles after flowback, and which PSU is tapped next.

articles.body:
Nvidia's results on Wednesday will test whether its latest Rubin chips can drive another period of explosive growth, at a moment when investors are questioning the sustainability of the AI spending boom. Analysts expect second-quarter revenue to nearly double year-on-year to $92.18 billion — the fastest growth in seven quarters — driven by a more than twofold increase in data centre sales, per LSEG. The stock has risen 11.8% this year, lagging major rivals, and briefly ceded its position as the world's most valuable company to Apple last month.

**The question is no longer demand, it is who is paying for it.** Nvidia has been pumping billions back into the AI ecosystem, raising concerns about circular deals that could artificially inflate demand and distort economic signals. This month it helped arrange $500 billion in financing from six major US financial institutions for customers building AI infrastructure. Last week it agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion to help OpenAI lease a data centre in Ohio for 20 years — one of its largest financing commitments. "This makes them a kind of central banking figure in the AI space," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, which holds the stock. "The real risk is total AI exposure with no diversification; the key for this to be successful is that adoption rates of AI tools must continue to grow." Big Tech data centre spending is set to exceed $730 billion this year, alongside ballooning outlays at smaller Nvidia-backed AI clouds such as CoreWeave. Investors are focused on how fast customers move from Blackwell to Vera Rubin, with shipments beginning this autumn.

**Which brings us to Hyderabad.** AM Intelligence — the AI infrastructure venture promoted by Greenko's founders — placed a binding order on Tuesday for 9,000 Nvidia Rubin GPUs, to be deployed as Vera Rubin NVL72 systems at a 30 MW facility in Hyderabad in the first quarter of 2027. The company says it will be among Asia's first frontier AI computing clusters on the Vera Rubin platform. Rubin, announced in January, can deliver up to ten times the agent throughput of Blackwell and costs 40-80% more.

The Hyderabad site is the first tranche of a planned 1 GW of Compute-as-a-Service capacity across India, the US, Finland and Malaysia, with 200 MW targeted near-term at capital expenditure exceeding $8 billion, inside a broader 5 GW development programme. Chairman Anil Chalamalasetty framed the logic: "For over two decades, we have focused on transforming electrons into value... Today, the electron-to-token opportunity allows us to take this capability further, converting power infrastructure into frontier AI compute at scale." The facilities use liquid cooling and are designed to accommodate successive generations of silicon.

**Read that pedigree carefully.** Greenko is a renewable energy and pumped-storage developer. Its founders' move into AI compute is the clearest statement yet that the binding constraint on AI infrastructure is power, not chips — and that whoever controls firm, dispatchable electricity has the strongest position in the value chain. That is the same insight underlying Adani Energy's Satara pumped-storage transmission win this week, and it is why Piyush Goyal is pitching India as a trusted data-centre destination citing $200 billion of investment commitments.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The listed proxies for India's AI build-out are power generation and transmission, data-centre real estate, and the EPC and cooling suppliers — not chip design. AMI is private, but its $8 billion near-term capex flows to exactly those counterparties. The risk is the one Mulberry named: if adoption disappoints, the capacity being financed today becomes stranded, and the debt behind it — including the convertible issuance sweeping through the AI-cloud sector — becomes the problem. Tonight's guidance is the market's next read on that.

**What to watch.** Nvidia's Rubin transition commentary and data-centre guidance, and whether Indian AI-infrastructure capex commitments convert into financial closure.

articles.body:
At the Hot Chips conference on Tuesday, OpenAI released the first benchmark results for Jalapeño, the inference chip it developed with Broadcom. Tested on SemiAnalysis's InferenceX benchmark, Jalapeño registered both more tokens per user and more throughput per kilowatt than currently available state-of-the-art inference processors. Against Nvidia's GB200 or GB300 superchips, OpenAI claims 1.5 to 1.9 times more AI work per watt across GPT-OSS 120B, DeepSeek R1 and Kimi K2.5 1T, with 1.7 to 3.6 times lower end-to-end latency.

"The bottom line is that the results show a very, very significant performance advance over state of the art," said Richard Ho, OpenAI's head of hardware. He framed the achievement as escaping a usual trade-off: "Jalapeño can serve more AI work per unit of power, while also returning responses more quickly. It's very efficient to serve a lot of customers, but it can also be very low latency."

**How they got there.** Jalapeño is an ASIC — purpose-built for inference rather than general-purpose compute — and OpenAI's own models assisted in its development. Because the company controls the full stack, it could target the specific phases where inference stalls: prefill, where the model ingests the prompt before producing anything, and inter-chip communication. "We designed Jalapeño to minimize data movement and communication delays," OpenAI wrote. "This means that model state, including the KV cache used while generating a response, can be explicitly placed and kept local while the system activates the right combination of compute, memory, and networking for each inference phase." The company plans to make Jalapeño a multigenerational platform where models, chips and memory are developed in concert.

**Three caveats, and they are large.** First, these are vendor-supplied benchmarks on a benchmark of the vendor's choosing, comparing against a competitor's current shipping product. Second — and Ho conceded this — Jalapeño deploys at the end of 2026 "in very small volumes", with meaningful volume in 2027. By then Nvidia will have shipped Vera Rubin, which it claims delivers up to ten times Blackwell's agent throughput. Comparing a 2027 chip to a 2026 competitor flatters the newcomer. Third, Ho said OpenAI does not expect to replace its entire chip lineup, describing Nvidia as among "very good partners". OpenAI is simultaneously benchmarking against Nvidia and depending on Nvidia to guarantee up to $105 billion of its Ohio data-centre lease.

**Why it matters anyway.** Inference is the recurring cost of the AI business and it scales with usage, unlike training, which is lumpy. Every point of efficiency compounds across billions of daily queries and translates directly into gross margin. If the largest inference buyer in the world can build its own silicon at a real efficiency advantage, the long-run pricing power of the merchant GPU vendor is capped — which is a live question for Nvidia investors on the day it reports. Perplexity's separate partnership with Nvidia this week to launch a fully local AI agent points the same direction: pushing inference to cheaper, more specialised hardware.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** No direct exposure, but a real second-order effect. Cheaper inference lowers the cost of building AI-native products, which is favourable for the Indian application-layer companies that Boundless VC and others are funding, and for IT services firms whose margins are being squeezed by AI-driven price deflation. It is less favourable for anyone assuming GPU scarcity persists indefinitely — including the AI data-centre developers now committing billions of dollars of capex to specific silicon generations.

**What to watch.** Independent third-party benchmarks, actual 2027 deployment volumes, and whether other large model providers follow OpenAI into custom inference silicon.

articles.body:
Nearly two years after SEBI launched measures to curb excessive retail speculation in derivatives, its own data says participation fell and behaviour did not.

**The findings.** The number of individual traders declined for the first time in nine years following the intervention. But 87.7% of individual traders ended FY26 with losses, and the average loss per trader rose over 2% to ₹1.16 lakh. Nearly 97% of retail activity remained concentrated in contracts with less than a week to expiry. And the composition of the decline is telling: while the active client count fell by about a fifth, equity derivatives turnover declined just 5%, with much of that accounted for by a sharp fall in individual futures turnover. Fewer people, trading roughly as much, in the same short-dated contracts, losing slightly more each.

**Why product-level curbs did not work.** SEBI's October 2024 intervention raised contract sizes, cut weekly expiries and tightened margins — all restrictions on the product. What the data suggests is that the marginal participant who left was the small one, while the behaviour of those who stayed was unchanged. One finding points to the fix: derivatives traders with larger underlying equity portfolios tend to fare better than those with little or no cash-equity exposure. That is an argument that the problem is not the instrument but who is using it.

**Which is why the industry is now asking for entry barriers.** "There is a need for some more stringent suitability exercises. I am an advocate of suitability," said Dhiraj Relli, MD and CEO of HDFC Securities, acknowledging partial success from earlier interventions while arguing more safeguards are needed. Proposals on the table include income thresholds, investor qualification tests and accredited-investor status. Former SEBI whole-time member Ananth Narayan framed the tension precisely: "How do we ensure, in a practical and proportionate way, that individuals taking leveraged risks understand those risks and have the financial capacity to bear potential losses? This deserves continued debate. The challenge is to improve investor protection without creating arbitrary barriers to participation."

Note who is asking. Brokers earn from derivatives volume, and they are requesting rules that would shrink their own client base. That is either genuine conviction or an expectation that regulation is coming anyway and it is better to shape it.

**The other structural change is settling in.** Tuesday was the first monthly Nifty expiry under the Closing Auction Session, introduced on 3 August to replace VWAP-based closing prices for the 208 F&O-eligible stocks, covering ₹10.11 trillion of linked AUM. Derivatives turnover was ₹569 trillion against ₹592 trillion on 28 July — down about 4%, and well below June's ₹750 trillion. "The first monthly expiry under the CAS has passed without a liquidity event, and that in itself is the headline," said Gaurav Arora, head of research at Sahi. "What has changed is its distribution through the session" — rollover and adjustment flow pulled forward, making 3:00-3:15pm one of the busiest windows. Arora notes the auction is currently dominated by passive funds, ETFs and high-frequency participants, with proprietary desks, arbitrageurs and retail largely stepping aside after 3:15pm.

That produces a quirk worth knowing. Tuesday's auction alone pushed the Nifty up 75 points and the Sensex up 126 points from their 3:15pm levels — catching many participants off guard, and helping the Nifty close at 24,334 (+115.50) and the Sensex at 77,656 (+286). Jefferies expects average daily turnover to recover from the second half of FY27 as CAS stabilises.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** If you trade F&O, the base rate is that you are in the 87.7%, and the one variable SEBI's data associates with better outcomes is holding a substantial cash-equity portfolio underneath the derivatives. Also: closing prices now move meaningfully in the final 20 minutes, so any strategy keyed to the close needs re-testing.

**What to watch.** Whether SEBI moves to suitability-based access, and CAS participation as arbitrageurs return.

Instagram's boss Adam Mosseri testified this week.
He admitted a tool meant to stop teens overusing the app was used by only 1-2% of accounts.
Meta did not publicly disclose how few people used it.
The states want about $200 billion, and Meta is reportedly discussing settling mid-trial.

articles.body:
Adam Mosseri, who has led Instagram since 2018, testified on Tuesday as the trial against Meta entered its second week — the biggest legal test yet of social media's effects on young users.

**The admission.** Under questioning from Jason Slothouber, a lawyer for Colorado, Mosseri acknowledged that the percentage of teenagers using "Take a Break" — a feature encouraging teen users to close the app after a period of use — was in the low single digits before Instagram made it the default. Pressed further, he put the figure at 1 or 2% of accounts, and confirmed Meta had not disclosed that low adoption.

**Why the 2021 number matters.** In a December 2021 blog post, Mosseri estimated that more than 90% of teenagers who turned the feature on kept it on. That statistic is true and almost entirely uninformative: it describes retention among the small group who opted in, not reach across the teen population. Presenting a 90%+ figure while the actual coverage was 1-2% is the specific kind of disclosure the states are building their case around — not a false statement, but a true one selected to create a false impression. Instagram did not make the feature default for teenagers until September 2024, nearly three years after launch, in the Teen Accounts rollout.

Mosseri denied the states' suggestion that Instagram had stalled. "Most teens didn't want it," he said. "We decided to push forward with it anyway."

**The case.** All 29 states allege Meta violated US federal law by improperly collecting and using the personal data of children under 13. Four — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — go further, accusing Meta of designing its platforms to hook young users, driving anxiety, depression and even suicide, while misleading consumers about safety. The states seek approximately $200 billion in damages. Meta rejects the accusations, saying its research showed no clear link between adolescent social media use and diminished wellbeing.

**The settlement signal.** Meta is reportedly discussing a mid-trial settlement as the case enters its second week, with Mint citing potential penalties running as high as $1.4 trillion in the worst case. A defendant that opens settlement discussions after testimony has begun is usually a defendant that has revised its estimate of how the remaining evidence will land. Mosseri is a central witness, and this was his first substantive day.

**Why the default question is the whole case in miniature.** Meta's defence is that it built safety tools and offered them. The states' argument is that offering a tool nobody uses is not a safety measure — that when a company knows adoption is 1-2% and leaves the setting off by default, it has made a product decision, not a neutral one. Every serious body of research on defaults, from organ donation to retirement savings, supports the states on the mechanism. Meta's own conduct supports it too: when it finally flipped the default in 2024, usage went from single digits to universal.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** No direct listed exposure, but three read-throughs worth tracking. First, a settlement or verdict at this scale would set the global reference point for platform liability on minors, and India's own regulatory direction on age-gating and children's data under the DPDP Act will be drafted with this outcome in view. Second, the same week brought Australia's data showing under-16 social media use rising after its ban, Brazil fining TikTok $30 million for child data violations, Australia securing a court-enforceable child safety undertaking from Roblox, and Norway moving on smart glasses — this is a coordinated global tightening, not a US anomaly. Third, any company building consumer products with teenage users should read the disclosure question, not just the design question: the exposure here came from how a number was reported.

**What to watch.** Whether a settlement is reached and at what figure, and the remaining Meta witnesses.

There are still reports of aggressive Chinese military positioning in Arunachal Pradesh.

articles.body:
National Security Advisor Ajit Doval held talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Tuesday in the 25th round of the Special Representatives dialogue, and the two sides agreed to continue working towards a "political settlement" of the boundary question "in the context of their overall and long-term interests", the Ministry of External Affairs said. The exchange was described as "candid and in-depth". India highlighted the importance of maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas for the continued development of the bilateral relationship.

The Indian embassy in Beijing said both sides "positively reviewed" the momentum in relations and "discussed ways to further expand bilateral cooperation, maintain stability and ensure peace and tranquility in the border areas, and make progress on boundary delimitation, while sustaining the ongoing work on transboundary cooperation". Before the border talks, Doval called on Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, who pointed to the two Xi-Modi meetings of the past two years — in Kazan and Tianjin — as having guided the relationship "back onto a track of recovery and improvement".

**Read the language carefully.** "Agreed to continue their work in seeking a political settlement" is not a settlement, and it is not new. What is new is the framing around delimitation and transboundary cooperation appearing in the readouts alongside the standard peace-and-tranquility formula — a hint that the technical track is being kept alive rather than parked. Doval, for his part, said normalcy in ties has been "a direct result of both sides maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas", which puts the causation the way India wants it: de-escalation first, then everything else.

**The counter-evidence sits in the same reporting.** The talks took place amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh. That is the recurring pattern of this relationship — diplomatic normalisation at the top table while the ground position is being tested. Neither track invalidates the other; both are real.

**The reason this is happening now.** Xi Jinping is expected in Delhi next month for the BRICS summit, his first trip to India since 2019. Reuters has reported an expected delegation of around 400 officials, business representatives and support staff, though there has been no official confirmation of the visit. Delegations of that size are not assembled for a summit photograph — they are structured for parallel discussions across ministries, regulators, business groups and sectoral agencies, which creates space for conversations on trade, manufacturing, technology and connectivity that a leaders' meeting alone cannot carry.

**Why it matters beyond bilateral ties.** BRICS has consistently struggled to convert ambition into action, and no internal division has mattered more than the India-China relationship — the bloc's two largest economies and the two members most capable of driving major initiatives. If the Delhi summit produces further bilateral movement, it removes the principal obstacle to BRICS taking concrete economic decisions rather than issuing political statements. Payment systems and agricultural commerce are expected on the agenda.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** Watch three channels. Direct investment approvals for Chinese firms in India, which have been restricted since 2020 and whose easing would matter for electronics and EV supply chains. Rare earths and critical mineral supply, where Beijing's leverage is currently being demonstrated against Washington — India's exposure is the same. And tourism, aviation and direct flight resumption, which typically follow political normalisation and would be the first visible commercial marker. The strategic backdrop is not simple: India is deepening maritime security cooperation with Japan and coordinating with the US in the Indian Ocean while normalising with Beijing.

**What to watch.** Official confirmation of Xi's visit, the delegation composition, and LAC reporting from Arunachal Pradesh.

articles.title: SpaceX plans a $100 billion Starship spaceport across 125,000 acres of Louisiana

It is designed for thousands of Starship launches every year, not a few dozen.
Building starts in 2027 and the first launch is planned for 2029.
SpaceX expects to create more than 3,000 jobs there.

articles.body:
SpaceX plans to invest up to $100 billion in Starbase Louisiana, a 125,000-acre spaceport it describes as the biggest launch site on Earth, expected to support thousands of Starship flights annually. Construction begins in 2027, with the first launch planned for 2029 and more than 3,000 jobs anticipated. "This will be a project like no other," the company said.

**The number to focus on is not $100 billion — it is "thousands of flights annually".** Global orbital launch activity across every country and operator has historically run in the low hundreds per year. A single site designed for thousands is not an incremental capacity addition; it is a bet that launch becomes a scheduled logistics service rather than a series of individually planned missions. Everything else in the announcement follows from that assumption. You need 125,000 acres because high-cadence operations require exclusion zones, propellant production and storage, vehicle integration and refurbishment at industrial scale, and enough separation to launch while another vehicle is being prepared.

**Why Louisiana, and why now.** The existing Starbase site in Boca Chica, Texas, is hemmed in by a wildlife refuge, a small community and the Mexican border, and its cadence is limited by environmental review and physical space rather than by engineering. Ars Technica separately reported this week that the world's busiest spaceport is about to get considerably quieter, at least temporarily — the industry is in the middle of a capacity reshuffle. Louisiana offers Gulf Coast access, existing heavy industrial and shipbuilding infrastructure, barge transport, and a state government willing to compete for the investment.

**Treat the capital figure as an intention, not a commitment.** "Up to $100 billion" over a build starting in 2027 with first launch in 2029 is a headline number attached to a multi-decade programme, and it will be spent only if Starship's flight rate and payload economics justify it. SpaceX has a strong record of eventually delivering on ambitious infrastructure and a consistent record of missing its stated timelines. The 2029 first launch should be read as an earliest case.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** No direct exposure, and this is not a trade. But it is a useful benchmark for anyone tracking India's own space commercialisation. ISRO and the private launch sector — Skyroot, Agnikul and the vendors around them — are competing in a global market where the cost curve is being set by whoever achieves the highest reusable cadence. India's structural advantage has been low-cost, high-reliability launch of modest payloads; a facility designed for thousands of annual Starship flights, if it works, compresses global price per kilogram to a level that erodes that advantage in the segments where the two overlap. It also matters for satellite operators: Starlink's second-generation 30,000-satellite constellation has just reapplied for IN-SPACe approval in India, and constellations of that size are only deployable with launch capacity of this kind. India's own regulatory decisions on satellite broadband are being taken against this backdrop.

**The broader pattern.** This is the third enormous private infrastructure commitment in a single week's news, alongside Nvidia arranging $500 billion of financing for AI data centres and AM Intelligence committing over $8 billion to Indian AI compute. Capital is concentrating in physical infrastructure — power, compute, launch — at a scale that used to be the preserve of states, and it is being raised in the same bond markets currently straining under $40 trillion of US government debt. These are not unrelated stories.

**What to watch.** Environmental and FAA approvals, Louisiana's incentive package, and Starship's actual flight cadence from Boca Chica between now and 2027.
