articles.body:
Four disclosures in 24 hours describe an Indian venture market funding conviction at the top and quietly liquidating the middle.

**Even Healthcare — ₹208 crore ($22mn) Series B led by Khosla Ventures.** The Bengaluru startup's board approved issuing 1,91,228 CCPS at ₹10,889.91 each. Khosla is putting in ₹145 crore, DLB Ventures ₹38.88 crore and Simon Fiduciaria ₹22.67 crore, with ADBEEV LLP and Better Capital at ₹1 crore each. Entrackr estimates the valuation at around $300 million. This is Even's second round this year — it raised $20 million in January led by Lachy Groom and Alpha Wave. Founded in 2020, it runs a membership-based healthcare model spanning primary care, diagnostics and hospital services, with care teams managing patients across consultation, diagnostics, hospitalisation and post-discharge recovery rather than treating each as a separate transaction. The FY25 financials are worth stating plainly: revenue ₹25.43 crore, up more than 4x from ₹6.24 crore, against losses of ₹90.15 crore, up 24.5%. A $300 million valuation on ₹25 crore of revenue is a bet on the model, not the numbers.

**Ringg AI — $10 million extension led by Peak XV.** With Arkam Ventures and Capital 2b participating, the round takes Ringg's Series A to $15.5 million after a $5.5 million first close in January. Founded by Siddharth Tripathi, Utkarsh Shukla and Kali Charan Vemuru, it began as text-to-speech company DesiVocal and pivoted to enterprise voice AI after finding speech-model development costs unsustainable — a pivot from the model layer to the application layer that mirrors the broader Indian bet. It processes around 20 million call attempts a month for Flipkart, Practo, Groww, Supernova, Goodscore and PolicyBazaar, covering outbound calling, lead qualification and loan collection, and is moving into healthcare appointment booking, e-commerce cart recovery and fintech KYC. Its agents are deployed across 1,200 Practo clinics. Voice is over 70% of the business, with chat, WhatsApp and browser agents being added. Capital goes to the platform, proprietary models and context graph, and enterprise go-to-market in India and abroad.

**Boundless VC — ₹300 crore ($35mn), oversubscribed.** "We decided we were going to do ₹300 crore, or $35 million. We were oversubscribed. We wanted to make sure we focused on pre-seed and seed," general partner Malpani told Mint. She led the generative AI thesis at Kae Capital previously. Her argument is that India has fallen behind the US and China on foundational models, that the opportunity sits at the application layer, and that the binding constraint is a shortage of local risk capital willing to write cheques before revenue and unit economics exist. "Globally, tech firms are raising multi-billion-dollar rounds on the basis of their background and ideas... We have to do the work at pre-seed and seed. We have to surface the companies, then they grow, and then growth funds will invest." The firm speaks to at least 1,000 founders a year.

**DealShare — looking for a buyer or a shutdown.** The grocery and household-essentials platform's board is weighing acquisition by online pharmacy TrueMeds or seafood e-retailer Captain Fresh; if neither materialises, it is likely to wind down. "DealShare does not have much of a business left to acquire. If the deal goes through, it would largely be a money-transfer transaction," one source said. Gross revenue fell to ₹432 crore in FY25 from ₹499 crore in FY24 and ₹1,963 crore in FY23 — a 78% collapse in two years — though losses narrowed to ₹87.65 crore. Over 100 employees were laid off in FY24 and the B2B vertical was shut. The latest CEO and CFO have left, and all four co-founders — Vineet Rao, Shankar Bora, Sourjyendu Medda and Rajat Shikhar — are gone. WestBridge Capital is a common investor with TrueMeds; Z47 with Captain Fresh.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The pattern: capital flows to AI applications with enterprise revenue and to healthcare models with visible retention, while first-generation quick-commerce and social-commerce businesses are being wound down or absorbed. Ringg's customer list — Flipkart, Groww, PolicyBazaar — is a useful signal about which listed and near-listed Indian companies are actually deploying AI in production rather than announcing it.

articles.body:
Three aviation policy items landed together, and the first is a structural change to how Indian airports are paid for.

**Hyderabad will charge arriving passengers.** The tariff regulator is changing how airport operators recover infrastructure costs, splitting the charge between arriving and departing passengers — making Hyderabad the first Indian airport to levy a User Development Fee on arrivals, both domestic and international.

**Why this is a bigger deal than the amount involved.** Indian airport economics have always been built on the departing passenger. The UDF is collected in the ticket price at origin, which means an airport's aeronautical revenue is a function of how many people leave from it, not how many use it. That is an odd basis for cost recovery, because an arriving passenger consumes real infrastructure — apron, baggage systems, terminal area, roads, air-conditioning — and pays nothing towards it. Airports with heavy inbound traffic have effectively been cross-subsidised by their own departing passengers.

Splitting the charge fixes that mismatch, and it does something else: it roughly doubles the passenger base an airport can bill against, which means the per-head fee needed to fund a given expansion falls. For a hub in the middle of a capex cycle, that materially changes the arithmetic. It is also, unavoidably, a new charge on flying into Hyderabad, and once one airport has it the precedent exists for every other operator's next tariff order. Expect Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and the new Navi Mumbai and Noida airports to seek the same treatment in their control periods.

**Second: random drug testing for every pilot.** The government is weighing annual random drug tests for all airline pilots. If extended to the full pilot population, India would be the first country in the world with such a norm. Current practice internationally is testing on reasonable suspicion, post-incident, or as part of the initial medical — not universal annual random screening. India already has among the more stringent breath-analyser regimes in commercial aviation. The operational questions are practical ones: who administers it, how rostering absorbs it, and what the appeal process looks like for a false positive that can end a career. Pilot unions will contest the details, not the principle.

**Third, and from further away: Luton Airport's operating rights are being prepared for sale.** The local-authority-owned company behind Britain's fifth-busiest aviation hub is readying a sale process for the right to operate the airport when the current deal expires in six years. Airport concession sales are one of the most reliable indicators of where global infrastructure capital thinks aviation traffic is heading, and Indian operators — GMR and Adani both — have looked at overseas concessions before.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** GMR Airports and Adani's airport portfolio are the listed exposure. A regulatory shift that broadens the billable passenger base is unambiguously positive for airport operators' revenue visibility, and it arrives just as the sector enters its heaviest capex phase in decades. The offset is airline economics: every rupee of UDF is a rupee on the ticket, and Indian aviation demand is price-elastic. With Air India seeking $1.5 billion from its owners this same week after a $2.33 billion loss, the industry has limited appetite for cost being pushed onto fares.

**For anyone working in or entering the sector.** The UDF change signals that Indian airport capex is accelerating rather than pausing, which is where the operational hiring is — terminal operations, ground handling, commercial and non-aeronautical revenue roles. The pilot-testing proposal signals a regulator willing to go beyond global norms on safety compliance, which expands the compliance and safety-management function at every carrier.

**What to watch.** The formal AERA order and the fee quantum, whether other airports file for the same split, and DGCA's consultation on the testing proposal.
